entries.0bfb828fc7be827c0112dd22d3b564a95cbc24c7: <div sID="gen10853" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="28" osisID="Ps.28" sID="Ps.28"/> <div eID="gen10853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10854" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10855" type="x-p"/> The former part of this psalm is the prayer of a saint militan and now in distress (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.1-Ps.28.3">ver. 1-3</reference>), to which is added the doom of God's implacable enemies, <reference osisRef="Ps.28.4-Ps.28.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. The latter part of the psalm is the thanksgiving of a saint triumphant, and delivered out of his distresses (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.6-Ps.28.8">ver. 6-8</reference>), to which is added a prophetical prayer for all God's faithful loyal subjects, <reference osisRef="Ps.28.9">ver. 9</reference>. So that it is hard to say which of these two conditions David was in when he penned it. Some think he was now in trouble seeking God, but at the same time preparing to praise him for his deliverance, and by faith giving him thanks for it, before it was wrought. Others think he was now in triumph, but remembered, and recorded for his own and others' benefit, the prayers he made when he was in affliction, that the mercy might relish the better, when it appeared to be an answer to them.
entries.466bfa1f2cc0136447762f934763fe1934de0c3c: <div eID="gen10855" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10854" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Prayer for Deliverance.</title> <div sID="gen10856" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Unto thee will I cry, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> my rock; be not silent to me: lest, <hi type="italic">if</hi> thou be silent to me, I become like them that go down into the pit. <hi type="super">2</hi> Hear the voice of my supplications, when I cry unto thee, when I lift up my hands toward thy holy oracle. 3 Draw me not away with the wicked, and with the workers of iniquity, which speak peace to their neighbours, but mischief <hi type="italic">is</hi> in their hearts. <hi type="super">4</hi> Give them according to their deeds, and according to the wickedness of their endeavours: give them after the work of their hands; render to them their desert. 5 Because they regard not the works of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , nor the operation of his hands, he shall destroy them, and not build them up. <div eID="gen10856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10857" type="x-p"/> In these verses David is very earnest in prayer. <div eID="gen10857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10858" type="x-p"/> I. He prays that God would graciously hear and answer him, now that, in his distress, he called upon him, <reference osisRef="Ps.28.1-Ps.28.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. Observe his faith in prayer: <hi type="italic">O Lord, my rock,</hi> denoting his belief of God's power (he is a rock) and his dependence upon that power—"He is <hi type="italic">my rock,</hi> on whom I build my hope." Observe his fervency in prayer: "<hi type="italic">To thee will I cry,</hi> as one in earnest, being ready to sink, unless thou come in with seasonable succour." And observe how solicitous he is to obtain an answer: <hi type="italic">"Be not silent to me,</hi> as one angry at my prayers, <reference osisRef="Ps.80.4">Ps. lxxx. 4</reference>. Lord, speak to me, answer me <hi type="italic">with good words and comfortable words</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.1.13">Zech. i. 13</reference>); though the thing I pray for has not been given me, yet let God speak to me joy and gladness, and make me to hear them. Lord, speak for me, in answer to my prayers, plead my cause, command deliverances for me, and thus hear and answer the voice of my supplications." Two things he pleads:—1. The sad despair he should be in if God slighted him: "<hi type="italic">If thou be silent to me,</hi> and I have not the tokens of thy favour, I am <hi type="italic">like those that go down into the pit</hi> (that is, I am a dead man, lost and undone); if God be not my friend, appear not to me and appear not for me, my hope and my help will have perished." Nothing can be so cutting, so killing, to a gracious soul, as the want of God's favour and the sense of his displeasure. <hi type="italic">I shall be like those that go down to hell</hi> (so some understand it); for what is the misery of the damned but this, that God is ever silent to them and deaf to their cry? Those are in some measure qualified for God's favour, and may expect it, who are thus possessed with a dread of his wrath, and to whom his frowns are worse than death. 2. The good hopes he had that God would favour him: <hi type="italic">I lift up my hands towards thy holy oracle,</hi> which denotes, not only an earnest desire, but an earnest expectation, thence to receive an answer of peace. The most holy place within the veil is here, as elsewhere, called the <hi type="italic">oracle;</hi> there the ark and the mercy-seat were, there God was said to <hi type="italic">dwell between the cherubim,</hi> and thence he spoke to his people, <reference osisRef="Num.7.89">Num. vii. 89</reference>. That was a type of Christ, and it is to him that we must lift up our eyes and hands, for through him all good comes from God to us. It was also a figure of heaven (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.24">Heb. ix. 24</reference>); and from God as our Father in heaven we are taught to expect an answer to our prayers. The scriptures are called <hi type="italic">the oracles of God,</hi> and to them we must have an eye in our prayers and expectations. There is the word on which God hath caused and encouraged us to hope. <div eID="gen10858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10859" type="x-p"/> II. He deprecates the doom of wicked people, as before (<reference osisRef="Ps.26.9">Ps. xxvi. 9</reference>, "<hi type="italic">Gather not my soul with sinners</hi>): Lord, I attend thy holy oracle, <hi type="italic">draw me not away</hi> from that <hi type="italic">with the wicked, and with the workers of iniquity,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.28.3">v. 3</reference>. 1. "Save me from being entangled in the snares they have laid for me. They flatter and cajole me, and speak peace to me; but they have a design upon me, for <hi type="italic">mischief is in their heart;</hi> they aim to disturb me, nay, to destroy me. Lord, suffer me not to be drawn away and ruined by their cursed plots; for they have, can have, no power, no success, against me, except it be given them from above." 2. "Save me from being infected with their sins and from doing as they do. Let me not be drawn away by their fallacious arguments, or their allurements, from the holy oracle (where I desire to dwell all the days of my life), to practise any wicked works;" see <reference osisRef="Ps.114.4">Ps. cxli. 4</reference>. "Lord, never leave me to myself, to use such arts of deceit and treachery for my safety as they use to my ruin. Let no event of Providence be an invincible temptation to me, to draw me either into the imitation or into the interest of wicked people." Good men dread the way of sinners; the best are sensible of the danger they are in of being drawn aside into it; and therefore we should all pray earnestly to God for his grace to keep us in our integrity. 3. "Save me from being involved in their doom; let me not be led forth with the workers of iniquity, for I am not one of those that speak peace while war is in their hearts." Note, Those that are careful not to partake with sinners in their sins have reason to hope that they shall not partake with them in their plagues, <reference osisRef="Rev.18.4">Rev. xviii. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen10859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10860" type="x-p"/> III. He imprecates the just judgments of God upon the workers of iniquity (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Give them according to their deeds.</hi> This is not the language of passion or revenge, nor is it inconsistent with the duty of praying for our enemies. But, 1. Thus he would show how far he was from complying with the workers of iniquity, and with what good reason he had begged not to be drawn away with them, because he was convinced that they could not be made more miserable then to be dealt with according to their deeds. 2. Thus he would express his zeal for the honour of God's justice in the governing world. "Lord, they think all well that they do, and justify themselves in their wicked practices. Lord, <hi type="italic">give them after the work of their hands,</hi> and so undeceive those about them, who think there is no harm in what they do because it goes unpunished," <reference osisRef="Ps.94.1-Ps.94.2">Ps. xciv. 1, 2</reference>. 3. This prayer is a prophecy that God will, sooner or later, render to all impenitent sinners according to their deserts. If what has been done amiss be not undone by repentance, there will certainly come a reckoning day, when God will render to every man who persists in his evil deeds according to them. It is a prophecy particularly of the destruction of destroyers: "<hi type="italic">They speak peace to their neighbours, but mischief is in their hearts;</hi> Lord, <hi type="italic">give them according to their deeds,</hi> let the spoilers be spoiled, and let those be treacherously dealt with who have thus dealt treacherously;" see <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Isa. xxxiii. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.6">Rev. xviii. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.10">xiii. 10</reference>. Observe, He foretels that God will reward them, not only according to their deed, but <hi type="italic">according to the wickedness of their endeavours;</hi> for sinners shall be reckoned with, not only for the mischief they have done, but for the mischief they would have done, which they designed, and did what they could to effect. And, if God go by this rule in dealing with the wicked, surely he will do so in dealing with the righteous, and will reward them, not only for the good they have done, but for the good they have endeavoured to do, though they could not accomplish it. <div eID="gen10860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10861" type="x-p"/> IV. He foretels their destruction for their contempt of God and his hand (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Because they regard not the works of the Lord and the operations of his hands,</hi> by which he manifests himself and speaks to the children of men, <hi type="italic">he will destroy them</hi> in this world and in the other, <hi type="italic">and not build them up.</hi>" Note, A stupid regardlessness of the works of God is the cause of their ruin. Why do men question the being or attributes of God, but because they do not duly regard his handiworks, which declare his glory, and in which the invisible things of him are clearly seen? Why do men forget God, and live without him, nay, affront God, and live in rebellion against him, but because they consider not the instances of that wrath of his which is revealed <hi type="italic">from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men?</hi> Why do the enemies of God's people hate and persecute them, and devise mischief against them, but because they regard not the works God has wrought for his church, by which he has made it appear how dear it is to him? See <reference osisRef="Isa.5.12">Isa. v. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen10861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10862" type="x-p"/> In singing this we must arm ourselves against all temptations to join with the workers of iniquity, and animate ourselves against all the troubles we may be threatened with by the workers of iniquity.
entries.ee531ce5da79b55da91fb7d7932bc90bb79ac856: <div eID="gen10862" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Devout Thanksgiving and Praise.</title> <div sID="gen10863" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , because he hath heard the voice of my supplications. <hi type="super">7</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> my strength and my shield; my heart trusted in him, and I am helped: therefore my heart greatly rejoiceth; and with my song will I praise him. <hi type="super">8</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> their strength, and he <hi type="italic">is</hi> the saving strength of his anointed. <hi type="super">9</hi> Save thy people, and bless thine inheritance: feed them also, and lift them up for ever. <div eID="gen10863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10864" type="x-p"/> In these verses, <div eID="gen10864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10865" type="x-p"/> I. David gives God thanks for the audience of his prayers as affectionately as a few verses before he had begged it: <hi type="italic">Blessed be the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.28.6">v. 6</reference>. How soon are the saints' sorrows turned into songs and their prayers into praises! It was in faith that David prayed (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.2">v. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">Hear the voice of my supplications;</hi> and by the same faith he gives thanks (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.6">v. 6</reference>) that <hi type="italic">God has heard the voice of his supplications.</hi> Note, 1. Those that pray in faith may rejoice in hope. "He hath heard me (graciously accepted me) and I am as sure of a real answer as if I had it already." 2. What we win by prayer we must wear by praise. Has God heard our supplications? Let us then bless his name. <div eID="gen10865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10866" type="x-p"/> II. He encourages himself to hope in God for the perfecting of every thing that concerned him. Having given to God the glory of his grace (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.6">v. 6</reference>), he is humbly bold to take the comfort of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.28.7">v. 7</reference>. This is the method of attaining peace: let us begin with praise that is attainable. Let us first bless God and then bless ourselves. Observe, 1. His dependence upon God: "<hi type="italic">The Lord is my strength,</hi> to support me, and carry me on, through all my services and sufferings. He is <hi type="italic">my shield,</hi> to protect me from all the malicious designs of my enemies against me. I have chosen him to be so, I have always found him so, and I expect he will still be so." 2. His experience of the benefits of that dependence: "<hi type="italic">My heart trusted in him,</hi> and in his power and promise; and it has not been in vain to do so, for <hi type="italic">I am helped,</hi> I have been often helped; not only God has given to me, in his due time, the help I trusted to him for, but my very trusting in him has helped me, in the mean time, and kept me from fainting." <reference osisRef="Ps.27.13">Ps. xxvii. 13</reference>. The very actings of faith are present aids to a dropping spirit, and often help it at a dead lift. 3. His improvement of this experience. (1.) He had the pleasure of it: <hi type="italic">Therefore my heart greatly rejoices.</hi> The joy of a believer is seated in the heart, while, in the laughter of the fool, the heart is sorrowful. It is great joy, <hi type="italic">joy unspeakable and full of glory.</hi> The heart that truly believes shall in due time greatly rejoice; it is <hi type="italic">joy and peace in believing</hi> that we are to expect. (2.) God shall have the praise of it: when <hi type="italic">my heart greatly rejoices, with my song will I praise him.</hi> This must we express our gratitude; it is the least we can do; and others will hereby be invited and encouraged to trust in him too. <div eID="gen10866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10867" type="x-p"/> III. He pleases himself with the interest which all good people, through Christ, have in God (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">The Lord is their strength;</hi> not mine only, but the strength of every believer." Note, The saints rejoice in their friends' comforts as well as their own; for, as we have not the less benefit from the light of the sun, so neither from the light of Gods' countenance, for others' sharing therein; for we are sure there is enough for all and enough for each. This is our communion with all saints, that God is their strength and ours, Christ their Lord and ours, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.2">1 Cor. i. 2</reference>. He is their strength, the strength of all Israel, because he is <hi type="italic">the saving strength of his anointed,</hi> that is, 1. Of David in the type. God, in strengthening him that was their king and fought their battles, strengthened the whole kingdom. He calls himself God's <hi type="italic">anointed</hi> because it was the unction he had received that exposed him to the envy of his enemies, and therefore entitled him to the divine protection. 2. Of Christ, his anointed, his Messiah, in the anti-type. God was his saving strength, qualified him for his undertaking and carried him through it; see <reference osisRef="Ps.89.21 Isa.49.5 Isa.50.7 Isa.50.9">Ps. lxxxix. 21; Isa. xlix. 5; l. 7, 9</reference>. And so he becomes their strength, the strength of all the saints; he strengthened him that is the church's head, and from him diffuses strength to all the members, has commanded his strength, and so <hi type="italic">strengthens what he has wrought for us;</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.68.28 Ps.68.80 Ps.68.17 Ps.68.18">Ps. lxviii. 28; lxxx. 17, 18</reference>. <div eID="gen10867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10868" type="x-p"/> IV. He concludes with a short but comprehensive prayer for the church of God, <reference osisRef="Ps.28.9">v. 9</reference>. He prays for Israel, not as his people ("save my people, and bless my inheritance"), though they were so, but, "<hi type="italic">thine.</hi>" God's interest in them lay nearer his heart than his own. <hi type="italic">We are thy people</hi> is a good plea, <reference osisRef="Isa.64.9">Isa. lxiv. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.19">lxiii. 19</reference>. <hi type="italic">I am thine, save me.</hi> God's people are his inheritance, dear to him, and precious in his eyes; what little glory he has from this world he has from them. <hi type="italic">The Lord's portion is his people.</hi> That which he begs of God for them is, 1. That he would save them from their enemies and the dangers they were exposed to. 2. That he would bless them with all good, flowing from his favour, in performance of his promise, and amounting to a happiness for them. 3. That he would <hi type="italic">feed them,</hi> bless them with plenty, and especially the plenty of his ordinances, which are food to the soul. <hi type="italic">Rule them;</hi> so the margin. "Direct their counsels and actions aright, and overrule their affairs for good. Feed them, and rule them; sets pastors, set rulers, over them, that shall do their office with wisdom and understanding." 4. That he would <hi type="italic">lift them up for ever,</hi> lift them up out of their troubles and distresses, and do this, not only for those of that age, but for his people in every age to come, even to the end. "Lift them up into thy glorious kingdom, lift them up as high as heaven." There, and there only, will the saints be lifted up for ever, never more to sink or be depressed. Observe, Those, and those only, whom God feeds and rules, who are willing to be taught, and guided, and governed, by him, shall be saved, and blessed, and lifted up for ever.  <chapter eID="Ps.28"/> <div eID="gen10868" type="x-p"/>

entries.aa76b9b1abaa3802c8280c9a029bae38670a7305: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5754"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 28</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.28.1-Ps.28.9">Psa 28:1-9</reference>. An earnest cry for divine aid against his enemies, as being also those of God, is followed by the Psalmist's praise in assurance of a favorable answer, and a prayer for all God's people.</title> <div sID="gen8757" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5754"/><hi type="bold">1. my rock--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.18.2">Psa 18:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.31">31</reference>).<div eID="gen8757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8758" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be not silent to me--</hi>literally, "from me," deaf or inattentive.<div eID="gen8758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8759" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">become like them, &c.--</hi>share their fate.<div eID="gen8759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8760" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">go down into the pit--</hi>or, "grave" (<reference osisRef="Ps.30.3">Psa 30:3</reference>). <div eID="gen8760" type="x-p"/>
entries.f524c9f0c03a91ba6cd5973319acb702044ef632: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5755"/><div sID="gen8761" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5755"/><hi type="bold">2. lift up my hands--</hi>a gesture of prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.4">Psa 63:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.141.2">141:2</reference>).<div eID="gen8761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8762" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">oracle--</hi>place of speaking (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.22">Ex 25:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.7.89">Nu 7:89</reference>), where God answered His people (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.5.7">Psa 5:7</reference>). <div eID="gen8762" type="x-p"/>
entries.3771064a706bc9cf61c16783244950969cf7ad5a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5756"/><div sID="gen8763" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5756"/><hi type="bold">3. Draw me not away--</hi>implies punishment as well as death (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.26.9">Psa 26:9</reference>). Hypocrisy is the special wickedness mentioned. <div eID="gen8763" type="x-p"/>
entries.ee2a193cdb69e69a7a993cb6d10d3eecf5f22162: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5757"/><div sID="gen8764" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5757"/>4. The imprecation is justified in <reference osisRef="Ps.28.5">Psa 28:5</reference>. The force of the passage is greatly enhanced by the accumulation of terms describing their sin.<div eID="gen8764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8765" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">endeavours--</hi>points out their deliberate sinfulness. <div eID="gen8765" type="x-p"/>
entries.e28661a1598e056de79043484638997e1625cc86: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5758"/><div sID="gen8766" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5758"/>5. Disregard of God's judgments brings a righteous punishment.<div eID="gen8766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8767" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">destroy ... build ... up--</hi>The positive strengthened by the negative form. <div eID="gen8767" type="x-p"/>
entries.ef6055ef1cd9caa92167b7bdeda30830e3ede7a6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5759"/><div sID="gen8768" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5759"/><hi type="bold">6. supplications--</hi>or, "cries for mercy." <div eID="gen8768" type="x-p"/>
entries.5a7a60ea5300c458db7db80118a3d3dad83b930f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5760"/><div sID="gen8769" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5760"/>7. The repetition of "heart" denotes his sincerity. <div eID="gen8769" type="x-p"/>
entries.9871e676946d8ee3985dd6646f78a89b40e23c4e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5761"/><div sID="gen8770" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5761"/>8. The distinction made between the people.<div eID="gen8770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8771" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their strength--</hi>and the anointed--may indicate Absalom's rebellion as the occasion. <div eID="gen8771" type="x-p"/>

The special prayer for the people sustains this view.<div eID="gen8772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8773" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">feed them--</hi>as a shepherd (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.1">Psa 23:1</reference>, &c.). <chapter eID="Ps.28"/>

entries.02ebbd296cdac2baa5dcfc13fb274f2dc92dfed8: <div eID="gen19422" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen19423" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19424" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19424" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19423" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19425" type="x-p"/> A righteous man in affliction makes supplication to God, and complains of the malice of his enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.28.1-Psa.28.4">Psa 28:1-4</reference>; whom he describes as impious, and whose destruction he predicts, <reference osisRef="Psa.28.5">Psa 28:5</reference>. He blesses God for hearing his prayers, and for filling him with consolation, <reference osisRef="Psa.28.6">Psa 28:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.28.7">Psa 28:7</reference>; then prays for God's people, <reference osisRef="Psa.28.8">Psa 28:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.28.9">Psa 28:9</reference>. <div eID="gen19425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19426" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is of the same complexion with the two preceding; and belongs most probably to the times of the captivity, though some have referred it to David in his persecutions. In the five first verses the author prays for support against his enemies, who appear to have acted treacherously against him. In the sixth and seventh he is supposed to have gained the victory, and returns with songs of triumph. The eighth is a chorus of the people sung to their conquering king. The ninth is the prayer of the king for his people. <div eID="gen19426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19427" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen19427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19428" type="x-p"/> O Lord my rock - צורי tsuri not only means my rock, but my fountain, and the origin of all the good I possess. <div eID="gen19428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19429" type="x-p"/> If thou be silent - If thou do not answer in such a way as to leave no doubt that thou hast heard me, I shall be as a dead man. It is a modern refinement in theology which teaches that no man can know when God hears and answers his prayers, but by an induction of particulars, and by an inference from his promises. And, on this ground, how can any man fairly presume that he is heard or answered at all? May not his inductions be no other than the common occurrences of providence? And may not providence be no more than the necessary occurrence of events? And is it not possible, on this skeptic ground, that there is no God to hear or answer? True religion knows nothing of these abominations; it teaches its votaries to pray to God, to expect an answer from him, and to look for the Holy Spirit to bear witness with their spirits that they are the sons and daughters of God.
entries.d99056de8b1c943ff76f3536fa1f77b284b90afe: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen19429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19430" type="x-p"/> Toward thy holy oracle - דביר קדשך debir kodshecha; debir properly means that place in the holy of holies from which God gave oracular answers to the high priest. This is a presumptive proof that there was a temple now standing; and the custom of stretching out the hands in prayer towards the temple, when the Jews were at a distance from it, is here referred to.
entries.410d13ef4271f20360e4fee36a511103c0a6d830: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen19430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19431" type="x-p"/> Draw file not away - Let me not be involved in the punishment of the wicked.
entries.bd9773f944e8bd3b522812a60b863c2c645177a2: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen19431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19432" type="x-p"/> Give them - Is the same as thou wilt give them; a prophetic declaration of what their lot will be.
entries.c59889be9a7007944dcca204f067d0562ecf9d95: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen19432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19433" type="x-p"/> They regard not the works of the Lord - They have no knowledge of the true God, either as to his nature, or as to his works. <div eID="gen19433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19434" type="x-p"/> He shall destroy them, and not build them up - This is a remarkable prophecy, and was literally fulfilled: the Babylonian empire was destroyed by Cyrus, and never built up again; for he founded the Persian empire on its ruins. haven the place where Babylon stood is now no longer known.
entries.58526f197d83d745916716cda728e8150a7cdf8d: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen19434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19435" type="x-p"/> The Lord is my strength - I have the fullest persuasion that he hears, will answer, and will save me.
entries.c0436bdb6bfde2a73f63564b1363c4196d59ba95: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen19435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19436" type="x-p"/> The Lord is their strength - Instead of למו lamo, to them, eight MSS. of Kennicott and De Rossi have לעמו leammo to his people; and this reading is confirmed by the Septuagint, Syriac, Vulgate, Ethiopic, Arabic, and Anglo-Saxon. This makes the passage more precise and intelligible; and of the truth of the reading there can be no reasonable doubt. "The Lord is the strength of his People, and the saving strength of his anointed." Both king and people are protected, upheld, and saved by him.
entries.55f89e2ecf3dff63373d07aa91f8d72c203056cd: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen19436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19437" type="x-p"/> Save thy people - Continue to preserve them from all their enemies; from idolatry, and from sin of every kind. <div eID="gen19437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19438" type="x-p"/> Bless thine inheritance - They have taken thee for their God; thou hast taken them for thy people. <div eID="gen19438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19439" type="x-p"/> Feed them - רעה raah signifies both to feed and to govern. Feed them, as a shepherd does his flock; rule them, as a father does his children. <div eID="gen19439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19440" type="x-p"/> Lift them up for ever - Maintain thy true Church; let no enemy prevail against it. Preserve and magnify them for ever. Lift them up: as hell is the bottomless pit in which damned spirits sink down for ever; or, as Chaucer says downe all downe; so heaven is an endless height of glory, in which there is an eternal rising or exaltation. Down, all down; up, all up; for ever and ever.  <chapter eID="Ps.28"/> <div eID="gen19440" type="x-p"/>

entries.d3178ba170df5c44d18033ef0104f4625035cbde: <div eID="gen9341" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Cry for Help and Thanksgiving, in a Time of Rebellion</title> <div sID="gen9342" type="x-p"/> To <reference osisRef="Ps.26.1-Ps.26.12">Psa 26:1-12</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.27.1-Ps.27.14">Psa 27:1-14</reference> a third Psalm is here added, belonging to the time of the persecution by Absolom. In this Psalm, also, the drawing towards the sanctuary of God cannot be lost sight of; and in addition thereto we have the intercession of the anointed one, when personally imperilled, on behalf of the people who are equally in need of help, - an intercession which can only be rightly estimated in connection with the circumstances of that time. Like <reference osisRef="Ps.27.1-Ps.27.14">Psa 27:1-14</reference> this, its neighbour, also divides into two parts; these parts, however, though their lines are of a different order, nevertheless bear a similar poetic impress. Both are composed of verses consisting of two and three lines. There are many points of contact between this Psalm and <reference osisRef="Ps.27.1-Ps.27.14">Psa 27:1-14</reference>; e.g., in the epithet applied to God, מעוז; but compare also <reference osisRef="Ps.28.3">Psa 28:3</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.26.9">Psa 26:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.28.2">Psa 28:2</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.31.23">Psa 31:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.28.9">Psa 28:9</reference> with Psa 29:11. The echoes of this Psalm in Isaiah are very many, and also in Jeremiah.
entries.28b69b6a3adf38834a2cc95411a3f334e8914cc6: <reference osisRef="Ps.28.1-Ps.28.5">Psa 28:1-5</reference> <div eID="gen9342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9343" type="x-p"/> This first half of the Psalm (<reference osisRef="Ps.28.1">Psa 28:1</reference>) is supplicatory. The preposition מן in connection with the verbs חרשׁ, to be deaf, dumb, and חשׁה, to keep silence, is a pregnant form of expression denoting an aversion or turning away which does not deign to give the suppliant an answer. Jahve is his צוּר, his ground of confidence; but if He continues thus to keep silence, then he who confides in Him will become like those who are going down (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.30">Psa 22:30</reference>), or are gone down (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.19">Isa 14:19</reference>) to the pit. The participle of the past answers better to the situation of one already on the brink of the abyss. In the double sentence with פּן, the chief accent falls upon the second clause, for which the first only paratactically opens up the way (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.5.4">Isa 5:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.12.1">Isa 12:1</reference>); in Latin it would be <hi type="italic">ne, te mihi non respondente, similis fiam</hi>. Olshausen, and Baur with him, believes that because ונמשׁלתּי has not the accent on the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi> as being <hi type="italic">perf. consec</hi>., it must be interpreted according to the accentuation thus, “in order that Thou mayst no longer keep silence, whilst I am already become like...” But this ought to be ואני נמשׁל, or at least נמשׁלתּי ואני. And if ונמשלתי were to be taken as a real perfect, it would then rather have to be rendered “and I should then be like.” But, notwithstanding ונמשׁלתּי is <hi type="italic">Milel</hi>, it is still <hi type="italic">perf</hi>. <hi type="italic">consecuticum</hi> (“and I am become like”); for if, in a sentence of more than one member following upon פן, the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>., as is usually the case (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.38.17">Psa 38:17</reference>), goes over into the <hi type="italic">perf</hi>., then the latter, in most instances, has the tone of the <hi type="italic">perf. consec</hi>. (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.19">Deu 4:19</reference>, Jdg 18:25, <reference osisRef="Prov.5.9-Prov.5.12">Pro 5:9-12</reference>, Mal 4:6), but not always. The <hi type="italic">penultima</hi>-accentuation is necessarily retained in connection with the two great pausal accents, <hi type="italic">Silluk</hi> and <hi type="italic">Athnach</hi>, <reference osisRef="Deut.8.12">Deu 8:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.9">Pro 30:9</reference>; in this passage in connection with <hi type="italic">Rebia mugrash</hi>, just as we may say, in general, the <hi type="italic">perf. consec</hi>. sometimes retains its <hi type="italic">penultima</hi>-accentuation in connection with distinctives instead of being accented on the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi>; e.g., in connection with <hi type="italic">Rebia mugrash</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.9">Pro 30:9</reference>; with <hi type="italic">Rebia</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.14">Pro 19:14</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.30.9">Pro 30:9</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ezek.14.17">Eze 14:17</reference>); with <hi type="italic">Zakeph</hi>. <reference osisRef="1Sam.29.8">1Sa 29:8</reference>; and even with <hi type="italic">Tiphcha</hi> Obad. Oba 1:10, Joe 3:21. The national grammarians are ignorant of any law on this subject.<note placement="foot">Aben-Ezra (<hi type="italic">Moznajim</hi> 36 <hi type="italic">b</hi>) explains the perfect accented on the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>. in <reference osisRef="Prov.30.9">Pro 30:9</reference> from the conformity of sound, and Kimchi (<hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 6 <hi type="italic">b</hi>) simply records the phenomenon.</note> <div eID="gen9343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9344" type="x-p"/> The point towards which the psalmist stretches forth his hands in prayer is Jahve’s holy דּביר. Such is the word (after the form בּריח, כּליא, עטין) used only in the Books of Kings and Chronicles, with the exception of this passage, to denote the Holy of Holies, not as being χρηματιστήριον (Aquila and Symmachus), or λαλητήριον, <hi type="italic">oraculum</hi> (Jerome), as it were, Jahve’s audience chamber (Hengstenberg) - a meaning that is not in accordance with the formation of the word, - but as the hinder part of the tent, from דּבר, Arabic <hi type="italic">dabara</hi>, to be behind, whence <hi type="italic">dubr</hi> (Talmudic דּוּבר), that which is behind (opp. <hi type="italic">kubl . kibal</hi>, that which is in the front), cf. <hi type="italic">Jesurun</hi> p. 87f. In <reference osisRef="Ps.28.3">Psa 28:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.28.4">Psa 28:4</reference> the prayer is expanded. משׁך (instead of which we find אסף in <reference osisRef="Ps.26.9">Psa 26:9</reference>), to draw any one down forcibly to destruction, or to drag him to the place of judgment, <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.20">Eze 32:20</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.10.8">Psa 10:8</reference>; Job 24:22. The delineation of the ungodly David borrows from his actual foes, Should he succumb to them, then his fate would be like that which awaits them, to whom he is conscious that he is radically unlike. He therefore prays that God’s recompensing justice may anticipate him, i.e., that He may requite them according to their desert, before he succumbs, to whom they have feigned שׁלום, a good understanding, or being on good terms, whereas they cherished in their heart the רעה that is now unmasked (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.9.7">Jer 9:7</reference>). נתן, used of an official adjudication, as in Hos 9:14; Jer 32:19. The <hi type="italic">epanaphora</hi> of תּן־להם is like Psa 27:14.<note placement="foot">This repetition, at the end, of a significant word that has been used at the beginning of a verse, is a favourite custom of Isaiah’s (<hi type="italic">Comment</hi>. S. 387; transl. ii. 134).</note> <div eID="gen9344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9345" type="x-p"/> The phrase השׁיב גּמוּל (שׁלּם), which occurs frequently in the prophets, signifies to recompense or repay to any one his accomplishing, his manifestation, that is to say, what he has done and merited; the thoughts and expression call to mind more particularly <reference osisRef="Isa.3.8-Isa.3.11">Isa 3:8-11</reference>; Isa 1:16. The right to pray for recompense (vengeance) is grounded, in <reference osisRef="Ps.28.5">Psa 28:5</reference>, upon their blindness to God’s just and merciful rule as it is to be seen in human history (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.5.12">Isa 5:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.11">Isa 22:11</reference>). The contrast of בּנה and חרס, to pull down (with a personal object, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.15.7">Exo 15:7</reference>), is like Jeremiah’s style (<reference osisRef="Ps.42.10">Psa 42:10</reference>, cf. 1:10; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.9">Psa 18:9</reference>, and frequently, Sir. 49:7). In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.28.5">Psa 28:5</reference></hi>, the prominent thought in David’s mind is, that they shamefully fail to recognise how gloriously and graciously God has again and again acknowledged him as His anointed one. He has (2 Sam 7) received the promise, that God would build him a house, i.e., grant perpetual continuance to his kingship. The Absolomites are in the act of rebellion against this divine appointment. Hence they shall experience the very reverse of the divine promise given to David: Jahve will pull them down and not build them up, He will destroy, at its very commencement, this dynasty set up in opposition to God.
entries.d75ad31949aeb722560f3f131609839dc712d572: <reference osisRef="Ps.28.6-Ps.28.9">Psa 28:6-9</reference> <div eID="gen9345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9346" type="x-p"/> The first half of the Psalm prayed for deliverance and for judgment; this second half gives thanks for both. If the poet wrote the Psalm at one sitting then at this point the certainty of being answered dawns upon him. But it is even possible that he added this second part later on, as a memorial of the answer he experienced to his prayer (Hitzig, Ewald). It sounds, at all events, like the record of something that has actually taken place. Jahve is his defence and shield. The conjoined perfects in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.28.7">Psa 28:7</reference></hi> denote that which is closely united in actual realisation; and in the <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. <hi type="italic">consec</hi>., as is frequently the case, e.g., in <reference osisRef="Job.14.2">Job 14:2</reference>, the historical signification retreats into the background before the more essential idea of that which has been produced. In משּׁירי, the song is conceived as the spring whence the הודות bubble forth; and instead of אודנּוּ we have the more impressive form אהודנּוּ, as in Ps 45:18; <reference osisRef="Ps.116.6">Psa 116:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.47">1Sa 17:47</reference>, the syncope being omitted. From suffering (<hi type="italic">Leid</hi>) springs song (<hi type="italic">Lied</hi>), and from song springs the praise (<hi type="italic">Lob</hi>) of Him, who has “turned” the suffering, just as it is attuned in <reference osisRef="Ps.28.6">Psa 28:6</reference> and Psa 28:8.<note placement="foot">There is a play of words and an alliteration in this sentence which we cannot fully reproduce in the English. - Tr.</note> <div eID="gen9346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9347" type="x-p"/> The αὐτοί, who are intended by למו in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.28.8">Psa 28:8</reference></hi>, are those of Israel, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.12.8">Psa 12:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.2">Isa 33:2</reference> (Hitzig). The lxx (κραταίωμα τοῦ λαοῦ αὐτοῦ) reads לעמּו, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.29.11">Psa 29:11</reference>, which is approved by Böttcher, Olshausen and Hupfeld; but למו yields a similar sense. First of all David thinks of the people, then of himself; for his private character retreats behind his official, by virtue of which he is the head of Israel. For this very reason his deliverance is the deliverance of Israel, to whom, so far as they have become unfaithful to His anointed, Jahve has not requited this faithlessness, and to whom, so far as they have remained true to him, He has rewarded this fidelity. Jahve is a עז a si evhaJ to them, inasmuch as He preserves them by His might from the destruction into which they would have precipitated themselves, or into which others would have precipitated them; and He is the מעוז ישׁוּעות of His anointed inasmuch as He surrounds him as an inaccessible place of refuge which secures to him salvation in all its fulness instead of the destruction anticipated. Israel’s salvation and blessing were at stake; but Israel is in fact God’s people and God’s inheritance - may He, then, work salvation for them in every future need and bless them. Apostatised from David, it was a flock in the hands of the hireling - may He ever take the place of shepherd to them and carry them in His arms through the destruction. The נשּׂאם coupled with וּרעם (thus it is to be pointed according to Ben-Asher) calls to mind <reference osisRef="Deut.1.31">Deu 1:31</reference>, “Jahve carried Israel as a man doth carry his son,” and <reference osisRef="Exod.19.4">Exo 19:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.11">Deu 32:11</reference>, “as on eagles’ wings.” The <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">Isa 63:9</reference>, is used of carrying the weak, whom one lifts up and thus removes out of its helplessness and danger. <reference osisRef="Ps.3.1-Ps.3.8">Psa 3:1-8</reference> closes just in the same way with an intercession; and the close of <reference osisRef="Ps.29.1-Ps.29.11">Psa 29:1-11</reference> is similar, but promissory, and consequently it is placed next to <reference osisRef="Ps.28.1">Psa 28:1</reference>-9.  <chapter eID="Ps.28"/> <div eID="gen9347" type="x-p"/>

entries.99b523bd924c6da54fb4723fc31c0a90f13dee2d:
PSALM 28.
After being delivered by God’s help from great dangers, David, in this psalm, according to his custom, first records the vows that he had made in the midst of his difficulties, and then his thanksgivings and praises to God, to induce others to follow his example. It is probable that he speaks of his persecutions by Saul.
A Psalm of David.
Psalm 28:1-2
1. Unto thee, O Jehovah! will I cry; O my strength! hold not thy peace from me; lest, shouldst thou be silent to me, I become like them that go down to the grave. 2. Hear the voice of my prayers when I cry to thee, when I lift up my hands to the sanctuary of thy holiness.
 
1. Unto thee, O Jehovah! will I cry. The Psalmist begins by declaring that he would betake himself to the help of God alone, which shows both his faith and his sincerity. Although men labor every where under a multitude of troubles, yet scarcely one in a hundred ever has recourse to God. Almost all having their consciences burdened with guilt, and having never experienced the power of divine grace which might lead them to betake themselves to it, either proudly gnaw the bit or fill the air with unavailing complaints, or, giving way to desperation, faint under their afflictions. By calling God his strength, David more fully shows that he confided in God’s assistance, not only when he was in the shade and in peace, but also when he was exposed to the severest temptations. In comparing himself to the dead, too, he intimates how great his straits were, although his object was not merely to point out the magnitude of his danger, but also to show that when he needed succor, he looked not here and there for it, but relied on God alone, without whose favor there remained no hope for him. It is, therefore, as if he had said, I am nothing if thou leavest me; if thou succourest me not, I perish. It is not enough for one who is in such a state of affliction to be sensible of his misery, unless, convinced of his inability to help himself, and renouncing all help from the world, he betake himself to God alone. And as the Scriptures inform us that God answers true believers when he shows by his operations that he regards their supplications, so the word silent is set in opposition to the sensible and present experience of his aid, when he appears, as it were, not to hear their prayers.

entries.db0f4d192bcfa212ea0404ce8550b66dec0829df:
<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="28" type="Psalm">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:443" />
                  <ns0:head>PSAL. XXVIII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:head>The ARGUMENT.</ns0:head>
                     <ns0:p>This <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> seems to be made upon the same Occasion with the former, and is mixed, as many others of his <ns0:hi>Psalms</ns0:hi> are, of Hopes and Fears, of Prayers and Praises.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:head>
                     <ns0:hi>A Psalm</ns0:hi> of David.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1. UNto thee will I cry, O LORD my rock, be not silent <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Be not deaf to my Prayers, nor dumb as to thy Answers to them.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> from me.</ns0:note> to me: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 143. 7.</ns0:note> lest <ns0:hi>if</ns0:hi> thou be silent to me, I become like them that go down into the pit <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Lest I be in the like or same Condition with them, (<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>)<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> A lost Creature: as I shall certainly be, if thou dost not succour me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2. Hear the voyce of my supplications, when I cry unto thee: when I lift up my hands <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> towards the Oracle of thy Sanctuary.</ns0:note> to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards thy holy oracle <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Towards the Holy of Holies, which is so called, 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 6. 23. Comp. with 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 3. 10. Compare also, 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 6. 5. and 8. 6. because there the Ark was; from whence God gave Oracular Answers to his People; and to which they accordingly directed their Prayers, not only when they drew near to it, but when they were at a distance from it, as <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 6. 10.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3. Draw me not away with the wicked <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The Sence is, Either, 1. Do not suffer me to be drawn away by their Counsel, or Example to imitate their evil Cour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ses. For God is oft said to do that which he doth not Effect, but only permit and Order, as 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 12. 12. Or, 2. Do not draw me into the same snares and mischief with them: do not drag me, as thou dost or wilst do all these Malefactors, to Execution, and Destruction. Let me not dye the Death of the wicked: Comp. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 26. 9. Thus <ns0:hi>drawing</ns0:hi> is used for drawing to Death. <ns0:hi>Iob.</ns0:hi> 21. 33. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 32. 20. This seems best to suit with the following Context, wherein he impre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cateth and foretelleth that Destruction upon his Enemies, which he deprecated for himself.</ns0:note>, and with the workers of iniquity: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 12. 2. & 55. 21. & 62. 4. Jer. 9. 8.</ns0:note> which speak peace to their neighbours, but mischief <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> in their heart <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Which are Hypocritical and perfidious Persons, whilst I through thy Grace am up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />right and sincere. Seeing then I am so unlike them in Dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />position and Practice, let me not be made like them in their Ruine.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4. Give them according to their deeds, and according to the wickedness of their endeavours <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> useth these Imprecations partly to Vindicate him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self from the slanders of his Enemies, who Reported him to be as wicked as they were, only more close and Cunning therein; which if he had been, he had bitterly Cursed himself; which it could not reasonably be presumed that he would do: Part<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, from his great and long Experience of their implacable and incorrigible Malignity, not only against him, but against God, and his declared Will, and against all truly good Men, and that covered with Pretences of Piety to God, and of Peaceableness towards their Neighbours, v. 3. which made their wickedness more inexcusable and detestable: Partly by the in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stinct and direction of God's Spirit, by whose inspiration he uttered this, as well as the rest of the Psalm, and Partly, that hereby he might provoke them to Repentance; for this Curse belongs only to those, who shall Obstinately persist in their wicked Courses. Add to all this, that as Verbs of the Im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />perative Mood, are oft used by the Hebrews for Futures, so these may not be proper Imprecations, but predictions of their Destruction.</ns0:note>: give them after the work of their hands, ren<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der to them their desert.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5. Because they regard not the works of the LORD, nor the operation of his hands <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) The providential works of God, both for and towards his Church and People in general; the serious Observation whereof would have made them afraid of opposing them, and desirous to joyn themselves with them: and for and to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wards me in particular, concerning whose Succession to the Kingdom, God hath so expressly declared his Mind and Will, and to whom he hath given so many, and such wonderful Pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />servations, that they who will not acknowledge it, but continue to oppose it, may well be presumed to be Guilty of Rebellion against God's Will, and of the Contempt of his Providence.</ns0:note>, he shall destroy them, and not build them up <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Destroy them utterly and irrecoverably; because they wilfully shut their Eyes against the Light of Gods Word, and Works.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6. Blessed <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> the LORD, because he hath heard <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">He speaks of it as past, either because God had in part heard, and answered him already: Or, because God assured him by his Spirit, that he had heard and accepted his Pray<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ers, and would assuredly answer him in due time.</ns0:note> the voyce of my supplications.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7. The LORD is my strength and my shield, my heart trusted in him, and I am help<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed: therefore my heart greatly rejoyceth, and with my song will I praise him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8. The LORD <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> his strength.</ns0:note> their strength <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) The strength of his people, mentioned in the next Verse: the Relative being put before the Antecedent, which is left to be gathered out of the following matter, as it is, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 24. 17. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 87. 1. Or, <ns0:hi>his strength:</ns0:hi> for the Hebrew Affix <ns0:hi>Mo,</ns0:hi> which commonly is plural, is sometimes taken sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gularly: of which see my Latin <ns0:hi>Synopsis</ns0:hi> here, and on <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 53. 8. And <ns0:hi>his, (i. e.</ns0:hi>) Of his anointed, as the next Clause ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plains it. Or, the Words may be thus rendred, <ns0:hi>strength is,</ns0:hi> Or, <ns0:hi>belongs to the Lord,</ns0:hi> Heb. <ns0:hi>The Lord, strength is his,</ns0:hi> Or, <ns0:hi>to him.</ns0:hi> It is an Hebrew Pleonasme.</ns0:note>, and he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> strength of Salvati<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> saving strength <ns0:hi>l</ns0:hi> of his anointed <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>The strength of the Preservations,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Deliverances,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Victories,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Salvations, (i. e.</ns0:hi>) He by whose strength alone he hath got these Victories, &c.</ns0:note>. <ns0:note place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>m (i. e.</ns0:hi>) Of me whom he hath anointed to be King, whom therefore he will defend, he speaks of himself in the third Per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son, which is usual in the Hebrew Tongue.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9. Save thy people, and bless thine inheri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tance <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> for whom I pray, Partly, because thou hast in some sort committed them to my Charge: and Partly, because <ns0:hi>Saul</ns0:hi> did not take due care of them.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> R<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> feed them also, and lift them up <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Raise them out of their low and afflicted Condition, in which they are, by reason of <ns0:hi>Sauls</ns0:hi> weakness and neglect, and by the prevailing power of the Phi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />listins, and advance them to a state of safety and Honour, and that not for a season, but with Constancy and Perpetuity, as it follows.</ns0:note> for ever.</ns0:p>
               </ns0:div>

Poole.heading:
PSAL. XXVIII. 
                     A Psalm of David.
